summary: Segment Routing encodes paths as sequences of segments that routing protocols advertise. This document extends the BGP Link State (BGP-LS) address family so Segment Routing information can be carried through BGP.

eli5.summary: Segment routing is like giving directions as a list of stops. This document lets those stops be shared through BGP-LS, which tells controllers what the network looks like.

questions: how does bgp-ls carry segment routing information
why does segment routing need bgp-ls
subtitle: How BGP carries Segment Routing labels and SIDs from IGP areas up to a controller.

tldr.problem: Segment Routing information is flooded by IS-IS, OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 only within one IGP area, so a controller cannot see segments across areas or autonomous systems using the IGP alone.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines new BGP-LS Attribute TLVs for nodes, links and prefixes that copy the SR data the IGPs already advertise, and leaves the BGP-LS NLRI encoding unchanged.
tldr.outcome: A controller or SR Path Computation Engine can collect SR information across an SR domain and build end-to-end paths. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 9356.

today: RFC 9085 is a Proposed Standard and is updated by RFC 9356. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why SR Needs BGP-LS
sections.content:
Segment Routing (SR) builds end-to-end paths from subpaths called segments. A segment can represent any instruction, topological or service based. Inside an IGP, segments are advertised as Segment Identifiers (SIDs) by IS-IS, OSPFv2 and OSPFv3.

The catch is scope. The IGP extensions for SR flood only within an IGP area, so the link-state database of one area is not enough to construct segments across multiple IGP areas or Autonomous System (AS) boundaries.

BGP-LS, defined in RFC 7752, already lets BGP carry link-state information. This document adds the SR-specific pieces so an external component, such as a controller, can collect SR information from across an SR domain and build the end-to-end path and SIDs to apply to an incoming packet.
sections.eli5: Each neighborhood of routers knows its own streets. A planner who wants to route a trip across many neighborhoods needs all those street lists in one place, and this document is how they get there.

sections.title: Collecting Link-State Data
sections.content:
In the typical deployment, one or more nodes in each IGP area are configured with BGP-LS. These BGP speakers form an Internal BGP mesh by connecting to one or more route reflectors, so the route reflectors obtain link-state information from all IGP areas, and from other ASes through External BGP peers. An external consumer connects to the route reflector, possibly moderated by a policy about what is advertised to it.

BGP-LS identifies each node, link or prefix by a key in the NLRI, and carries its properties in the BGP-LS Attribute. This document adds new TLVs to that attribute and, importantly, does not change the encoding of the BGP-LS NLRIs.

SR operates within a trusted domain, which is a single AS or several ASes managed by the same administrative entity, such as one provider network.
sections.eli5: Helpers in each neighborhood send their notes to a few central post offices, and the planner reads from the post office. The notes are new, but the envelopes stay the same.

sections.title: Node Attribute TLVs
sections.content:
Five TLVs describe a node and belong only in the BGP-LS Attribute of the Node NLRI for the IGP node that originates the matching IGP TLV or sub-TLV. In every case the information is derived from the protocol-specific IGP advertisements.

  • SID/Label (type 1161) is used as a sub-TLV. A length of 3 means a label held in the 20 rightmost bits (total size 7); a length of 4 means a 32-bit SID (total size 8).
  • SR Capabilities (1034) advertises the node's Segment Routing Global Base (SRGB) ranges. Each entry has a 3-octet non-zero Range Size and a SID/Label sub-TLV for the first label, which can only be label-encoded here.
  • SR Algorithm (1035) lists the algorithms the node supports, one octet each.
  • SR Local Block (1036) gives the label ranges reserved for local SIDs such as Adjacency SIDs, so controllers know which local SIDs are available.
  • SRMS Preference (1037) carries an unsigned 8-bit preference for Segment Routing Mapping Server advertisements.

For the Flags field of SR Capabilities and SR Local Block, IS-IS flags apply; for OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 the flags are not defined and MUST be set to 0 and ignored on receipt.
sections.eli5: A node's card says which number ranges it uses for its labels, which route-picking methods it knows, and how much to trust its address book. Each item on the card has its own code number.

sections.title: Link Attribute TLVs
sections.content:
Three TLVs go with the Link NLRI of the IGP node that originates the corresponding IGP data.

  • Adjacency SID (1099) describes an Adjacency SID with Flags, a one-octet Weight used for load balancing, 2 reserved octets that MUST be 0, and a SID, label or index. Its length is 7 or 8 octets.
  • LAN Adjacency SID (1100) lets a node announce adjacencies to all other nodes on a LAN in one Link NLRI. Without it, a separate Link NLRI would be needed for each extra adjacency. It adds a neighbor ID of 6 octets (IS-IS System ID) or 4 octets (OSPF Router-ID).
  • L2 Bundle Member Attributes (1172) identifies a member link of a bundle through a 4-octet link-local identifier, with link attributes carried as sub-TLVs. It is derived from IS-IS, and the RFC says equivalent functionality has not been specified for OSPF.

The Flags and the SID field are interpreted according to the underlying IS-IS, OSPFv2 or OSPFv3 protocol, and the Protocol-ID of the Link NLRI tells the parser which one applies.
sections.eli5: Each road between routers can have its own sign: a name tag for the road, a tag for each neighbor on a shared street, and a tag for each lane in a bundle of lanes.

sections.title: Prefix Attribute TLVs
sections.content:
Five TLVs go with the Prefix NLRI of the IGP node that originates the corresponding prefix data.

  • Prefix-SID (1158) carries Flags, a one-octet Algorithm, 2 reserved octets and a SID, label or index, in 7 or 8 octets.
  • Prefix Attribute Flags (1170) carries the IPv4/IPv6 prefix attribute flags in a variable-length field.
  • Source Router Identifier (1171) holds the 4- or 16-octet IPv4 or IPv6 router identifier of the prefix originator.
  • Source OSPF Router-ID (1174) holds the 4-octet OSPF Router-ID of the originator and applies only to OSPF.
  • Range (1159) advertises a range of prefix-to-SID mappings for the SRMS function. Its Range Size is 2 octets and counts the prefixes covered. A Prefix NLRI with a Range TLV counts as a normal routing prefix only when an IGP metric TLV (1095) is also associated with it.

Sections 2.4 and 2.5 of the RFC add tables mapping each BGP-LS TLV to its IS-IS, OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 equivalent.
sections.eli5: Each destination address can carry a label, some notes about itself, the name of the router that announced it, and, for a whole group of addresses, a single shared rule.

sections.title: Manageability
sections.content:
The new TLVs do not affect BGP operations beyond what RFC 7752 already covers. The syntactic malformed-attribute checks from RFC 7752 now include the new TLVs, and a syntax error in them causes the BGP-LS Attribute to be discarded with an error log.

Semantic checking of the TLVs, and of how they relate to the NLRI types, is left to the consumer, such as an application or controller, not to BGP. A consumer like an SR Path Computation Engine can use the data for SR-based traffic engineering, and errors in encoding or decoding may leave it without information or with incorrect information. The document introduces no new configuration or monitoring aspects.
sections.eli5: If a note is written in a broken way, the post office throws it out and writes it in a log. Checking whether the note makes sense is the planner's job.

sections.title: IANA Code Points
sections.content: IANA registered the TLV code points in the BGP-LS Node Descriptor, Link Descriptor, Prefix Descriptor, and Attribute TLVs registry. The registry's IS-IS TLV/Sub-TLV column is left empty for these entries. The summary table in the RFC lists 14 code points, and the visual below reproduces them.
sections.eli5: The numbers for each new tag were written in the official list so everyone uses the same ones.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The extensions, by themselves, do not change the BGP-LS security model of RFC 7752, and its security considerations also apply. The IGP instances that originate the data are assumed to support the security and authentication mechanisms of the IGP specifications.

SR operates within a trusted domain, so link-state information, including SR information, should reach only consumers within it. BGP sessions for other address families may be set up to routers outside the SR domain, so the RFC recommends isolating BGP-LS peering sessions so that topology information is not advertised to an external BGP session outside the SR domain.
sections.eli5: The map is only for people inside the club. Keep the map-sharing line separate from lines that go to strangers.
